concepts.title: Maintenance & running costs
concepts.summary: Drivetrain choices, wear parts, servicing and battery life over three years.
concepts.overview: This topic collects what the bike will cost to keep running over three years at about 6,000 km a year. Chain bikes need about five chains, a couple of cassettes, brake pads and two services a year, roughly 850 in total. A [belt drive](#c/01M3VW6A4ZMJQZTS6MHQ460VJS) on an [internal gear hub](#c/01M3VW6A4ZK3TSVVEHX6D3AHQ9) brings that to about 650, so it saves only around 200 (see [is a belt drive worth it?](#c/01M3VW6A50XWGZPKC7748BFKS1)). These figures leave out the battery, which keeps about 80 percent of capacity after 500 to 800 full cycles and may need a 600 to 800 replacement near year three or four. See [three-year running cost](#c/01M3VW6A50HE7E988Q791BPPFQ) for the breakdown.

overviewProv.quote: So the belt saves maybe 200 over three years, not a huge amount.

concepts.title: My commute & situation
concepts.summary: The reader's commute, body, budget and home constraints that shape the choice.
concepts.overview: This topic collects the facts about the reader that drive the whole decision, as distinct from the bikes. It covers [Me](#c/01M3VW4MRM8EAH31QW3SDKRBNA) (about 80 kg, carrying a laptop bag, wanting to arrive unsweaty), [the commute](#c/01M3VW4MRMA6ZDK9PFK3QVG66D) of 14 km each way with a hill, the goal of [arriving without sweating](#c/01M3VW4MRMXKGXJ0AMBXTETEB9), and [Second floor, no lift](#c/01M3VW4MRN65TXTP8RWDCGY48F). The budget of up to 3,500 is part of the same picture. Together these explain why a mid-drive was favoured, why 400–500 Wh is enough, and why weight and theft later became criteria. Reading it first makes the comparisons of bikes easier to follow.

concepts.title: Theft protection
concepts.summary: Ways to protect a bike left at a work rack: removable battery, locks, motor lock, insurance.
concepts.overview: Theft matters here because the reader would leave the bike at a rack at work all day, so protection has to be planned alongside the purchase. The assistant laid out four layers. A [removable battery](#c/01M3VW6A51Y2W9DMNYQDV2M5KS), which all four shortlisted bikes have, can be taken inside. A Sold Secure Gold or Diamond [D-lock plus cable](#c/01M3VW6A51NF5NMYW5N1V8GPQM) secures the frame and the front wheel. The [app motor lock](#c/01M3VW6A514F2A1300M3DT9SJT) can disable the motor when you walk away; the Alder supports it and the Cedar doesn't. Finally, [bike insurance](#c/01M3VW6HBZZ0PWT237K2HFXTDB) runs around 100 to 150 a year for a 3,000 bike. These count heavily in the choice, because the motor lock is what puts the Alder ahead on this criterion. The lock and insurance are recommended but not yet decided.

concepts.title: Me
concepts.summary: Commuter, about 80 kg, riding 14 km each way with a laptop bag; budget up to 3,500; lives on the second floor with no lift.
concepts.overview: This Expedition is built around one person: a commuter of about 80 kg who rides 14 km each way with a laptop bag, has a budget of up to 3,500, and lives on a second floor with no lift. Those facts, not a generic rider profile, drive every judgement here. The weight and the one steep hill make torque matter, so they point toward a mid-drive. The stairs make the bike's carry weight a real criterion. The bike will sit at a rack at work, which is why theft protection gets so much attention. All of this is gathered in [My commute & situation](#c/01M3VW3XZ8BMKGWK9A74VTN663), and it is what raises the central question, [Which e-bike should I buy?](#c/01M3VW4MRNRXV5FKBXX0X4Q544).

concepts.title: Motor torque
concepts.summary: The number to compare for hill climbing: 60–85 Nm for mid-drives (Bosch CX 85, Shimano EP8 85, Bosch Performance Line 75) vs 40–50 Nm for hub motors.
concepts.overview: Torque, measured in newton-metres (Nm), is the number to look at when judging how well an e-bike motor climbs. Mid-drives typically give 60 to 85 Nm, with the Bosch Performance Line CX and Shimano EP8 at 85 Nm and the Bosch Performance Line at 75 Nm, while typical hub motors give only 40 to 50 Nm. It matters here because of the one hill, about 800 m at up to 8 percent, and the reader's wish not to arrive sweaty. A [mid-drive motor](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) with high torque lets you shift down and keep cadence, which is why torque feeds directly into [hill climbing](#c/01M3VW59EVTDPBDCFA6HP66A99). For this hill, 75 Nm is plenty, so the highest figure is not essential.

concepts.title: Frame style
concepts.summary: Step-through is easier with a bag and in work clothes; a diamond frame is stiffer and lighter.
concepts.overview: Frame style is one of the three early choices, alongside motor and battery. A step-through frame is easier to get on and off with a bag and in work clothes, while a diamond frame is stiffer and lighter. For this reader the lower weight of a diamond frame counts in its favour because of [Second floor, no lift](#c/01M3VW4MRN65TXTP8RWDCGY48F), while the step-through's convenience suits a laptop bag and office clothes. The assistant did not settle the question, but fit is concrete enough to check in person: the [Test-ride checklist](#c/01M3VW6A52YXHZH1AJX1277NYM) asks the reader to stand over the frame with a few centimetres of clearance and reach the bars without locking the elbows. It is covered in [Motor, battery & frame basics](#c/01M3VW3XZ86KW12PX2EMYD4SJC).

concepts.title: Hub motor
concepts.summary: Motor in the rear or front wheel; cheaper, quieter, less maintenance, but struggles on long steep climbs. Typically 40–50 Nm.
concepts.overview: A hub motor sits in the rear or front wheel instead of at the pedals. It is cheaper, quieter and needs less maintenance than a mid-drive, but it does not work through the bike's gears, and typical units give only 40 to 50 Nm of torque, so it struggles on long steep climbs. For this commuter the question was the single 800 m hill at up to 8 percent: a good hub motor can manage that at moderate speed, but a [mid-drive motor](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) lets you shift down and keep cadence, which means less effort and less sweat. The [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3VW59EVFKQ96MWZWNKBPFN0) is the example in the shortlist, included for contrast and set aside early.

overviewProv.quote: a mid-drive lets you shift down and keep cadence, which means less effort and less sweat

concepts.title: Dogwood Hub
concepts.summary: Hub-motor contrast option: 45 Nm rear hub, 418 Wh, 7-speed, 21 kg, around 1,700; not worth comparing closely.
concepts.overview: The Dogwood Hub is the one bike on the shortlist that is not a mid-drive. It has a 45 Nm rear [hub motor](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT), a 418 Wh battery, 7 speeds and weighs 21 kg, the lightest of the four, at about 1,700, the cheapest. The assistant included it for contrast. It only partly meets [hill climbing](#c/01M3VW59EVTDPBDCFA6HP66A99): 8 percent over 800 m is manageable at moderate speed, but it takes more effort and so more sweat, which the reader wants to avoid. It was set aside early, and the assistant said the first three bikes were the ones worth comparing closely.

concepts.title: Light enough for the stairs
concepts.summary: Carrying it up two flights daily: 23–24 kg is noticeably easier than 26 kg; removing the battery saves 2.5–3 kg.
concepts.overview: This criterion comes from a practical fact: the reader lives on the second floor with no lift and will carry the bike up two flights every day. That makes weight a hard requirement rather than a preference. Between 23 and 24 kg the bike is noticeably easier to carry than at 26 kg, and taking the battery out first saves another 2.5 to 3 kg. The [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD) at 23 kg is best and the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) at 24 kg is close, while the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR) at 26 kg is the heaviest mid-drive. It is the reason the belt-drive bike loses ground, and it is something to confirm on the test ride by carrying the bike up a flight with the battery out.

concepts.title: Is a belt drive worth it?
concepts.summary: Worth it for a daily rain commuter who won't clean a chain, but it saves only about 200 over three years and brings internal-hub trade-offs.
concepts.overview: The reader asked this after seeing that the Birch Metro 8 uses a [belt drive](#c/01M3VW6A4ZMJQZTS6MHQ460VJS). A belt needs no oil, doesn't rust and lasts two to three times as long as a chain, which suits a daily commuter who rides in rain and doesn't want to clean a chain. The trade-offs are an internal gear hub with fewer gears and slightly more friction, repairs that need a shop that knows them, and a fiddlier flat rear tyre. The money case is modest: over three years the running cost is about 650 against 850 for chain bikes, so [the belt saves only about 200](#c/01M3VW6A50SW9N8XW6VA4F522F). Its real appeal is [low maintenance](#c/01M3VW59EVWQ45SDAZ1Z49QGK9). For this reader it also adds weight, as the Birch is the heaviest mid-drive at 26 kg.

concepts.title: Internal gear hub
concepts.summary: Gears sealed inside the rear hub; required for a belt. Fewer gears, slightly more friction, needs a knowledgeable shop, fiddlier rear-flat repair.
concepts.overview: An internal gear hub (IGH) packs the bike's gears inside a sealed rear hub instead of leaving them as exposed cogs on a cassette. That sealing is why it needs so little attention, and it is also what makes a [belt drive](#c/01M3VW6A4ZMJQZTS6MHQ460VJS) possible: a belt can't shift across cassette cogs, so it only works with a hub like this. The [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR) uses a Nexus 5 hub for exactly this reason. The trade-offs are fewer gears, slightly more friction, repairs that need a shop that knows these hubs, and a fiddlier job when the rear tyre goes flat. For this commuter it is the price paid for lower upkeep, and it counts toward the [Maintenance & running costs](#c/01M3VW3XZ9EGS54338YDQ9KP53) picture.

concepts.title: Bosch & Shimano systems
concepts.summary: Rated by independent tests as more refined: smoother power, better sensors and software, and a larger dealer network for warranty repairs.
concepts.overview: Bosch and Shimano are the two established mid-drive systems in this comparison. Independent tests generally rate them as more refined than the alternatives, with smoother power delivery, better sensors and software, and a larger dealer network for warranty repairs. The torque figures from the chat, such as 85 Nm for the Bosch Performance Line CX and Shimano EP8, and 75 Nm for the Bosch Performance Line, show they cover the range the hill needs. The [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) uses Bosch and the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR) uses Shimano. They are the main alternative to [Bafang systems](#c/01M3VW6A51SBKZF5FW2TJ05CXA), which are cheaper but less polished. The dealer network is the strongest argument for them, as in [dealer network matters most](#c/01M3VW6A5155D0KHWTABVDSBPC).

concepts.title: App motor lock
concepts.summary: Bosch's eBike Lock via the Flow app disables the motor when you walk away; the Alder supports it, the Cedar doesn't.
concepts.overview: The app motor lock is a Bosch feature, the eBike Lock used through the Flow app, that disables the motor when you walk away. It doesn't stop someone carrying the bike off, but it makes a stolen bike far less useful and adds a layer beyond the physical lock. For a reader who will leave the bike at a work rack, it is the Alder's main theft edge: the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) supports it and the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD) doesn't. It feeds directly into [Theft resistance](#c/01M3VW59EV784C6QXRWRRR0XS6) and is one reason the Alder was favoured. Because it is untested, the [Test-ride checklist](#c/01M3VW6A52YXHZH1AJX1277NYM) says to try it in the app before buying.

concepts.overview: Before comparing individual bikes, the assistant named three choices that shape everything else: the motor, the battery and the frame. The motor is the biggest fork, between a [mid-drive](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) at the pedals, which climbs better, and a [hub motor](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT) in the wheel, which is cheaper and quieter. [Motor torque](#c/01M3VW4MRPPQT6XRYW092NBN8G) is the number that compares them on hills. The [battery capacity](#c/01M3VW4MRPEP5GMFXZW4JEEA8D) matters for a 28 km daily ride: 400 to 500 Wh gives a couple of days between winter charges. The [frame style](#c/01M3VW4MRPAJQRZ9WKVZC1TXH7) is step-through, easier in work clothes with a bag, or diamond, stiffer and lighter. concepts.overview: The Cedar Urban is the budget mid-drive in the shortlist: a Bafang M400 with 80 Nm of torque, a 460 Wh battery, a 9-speed chain drive, 23 kg, and around 2,300. Its torque sits among the strongest for the hill. The compromises are a chain that needs regular care, less polished power from [Bafang systems](#c/01M3VW6A51SBKZF5FW2TJ05CXA), and no app motor lock, so theft protection rests on the battery and locks alone. concepts.title: Motor drives through the bike's gears
concepts.summary: A mid-drive drives the chain, so you can shift down on a climb and keep cadence: less effort, less sweat.
concepts.overview: A mid-drive motor sits at the pedals and drives the chain, so its power runs through the bike's own gears. That is the reason it climbs better than a hub motor, which drives the wheel directly. On a hill you can shift down and keep a steady, comfortable cadence, so the motor works in its efficient range and you put in less effort and sweat less. This matters for the reader, who has an 800 m hill at up to 8 percent and does not want to arrive sweaty. It is why the assistant called [mid-drive the safer bet](#c/01M3VW4MRPEF6FXC20G7PPVN3P), and it improves [hill climbing](#c/01M3VW59EVTDPBDCFA6HP66A99). See [Mid-drive motor](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) for where it sits and how it differs from a hub.

concepts.title: Quiet ride
concepts.summary: How quietly the motor runs while riding; hub motors are the quieter type.
concepts.overview: Quiet ride is how little noise the motor makes while you pedal. In this Expedition it turns up only once, in the first overview of motor types, where a [hub motor](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT) is described as cheaper, quieter and lower-maintenance than a mid-drive. That is a small point in the hub's favour. A mid-drive works through the bike's chain and gears, so it tends to be a little louder. Quietness is not on the reader's stated priority list, which is hill climbing, low maintenance, carry weight and theft protection, with price second. It therefore never decided anything. The hub bike it favours, the Dogwood Hub, was set aside early because a 45 Nm motor is weak for an 800 m hill at 8 percent. The reader can still listen for motor noise on the test ride, but it should not outweigh climbing ability.

concepts.title: Hill climbing
concepts.summary: Handling the 800 m, 8% hill without effort; measured by torque.
concepts.overview: Hill climbing is the reader's top criterion: handling one real hill, about 800 m long and up to 8 percent, without arriving sweaty. It is judged mainly by [motor torque](#c/01M3VW4MRPPQT6XRYW092NBN8G). The Birch (85 Nm) and Cedar (80 Nm) are strongest, and the Alder's 75 Nm is plenty for an 8 percent grade. A hub motor like the Dogwood's 45 Nm can manage that hill at moderate speed, but with more effort. A [mid-drive](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) also helps because it works through the gears, so the rider can shift down and keep cadence. That is why this criterion shaped the early choice of motor type, and why the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) still meets it despite having the lowest torque of the three mid-drives. The test ride on a similar hill in mid assist is the real check.

That weight is a real problem for a reader who carries the bike up to a second-floor flat daily, and for theft it relies on locks and a removable battery alone. It is the bike to choose if low maintenance matters more than the stairs. But [the belt saves only about 200](#c/01M3VW6A50SW9N8XW6VA4F522F) over three years, so the reader went with the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH). Specs and price are approximate.

concepts.title: Brands & drive systems
concepts.summary: How Bosch, Shimano and Bafang systems compare, and whether battery brand matters.
concepts.overview: This topic gathers the question of which motor system to trust: [Bosch and Shimano systems](#c/01M3VW6A51630KP5K96DHA0A42) against [Bafang systems](#c/01M3VW6A51SBKZF5FW2TJ05CXA). The reader's starting point was a belief that Bosch batteries beat Bafang ([the question](#c/01M3VW6A50Q6JMABF6NW443DKY) and [the claim](#c/01M3VW6A50GWTHXRYE9GFPBEBN)). The answer was only partly: most brands use cells from the same few makers, so the battery is a weak argument, while refined power delivery and a larger dealer network are real advantages for Bosch and Shimano. concepts.title: Dealer network matters most
concepts.summary: For a daily commuter where downtime matters, the dealer network for warranty repairs is the real reason to prefer Bosch, more than the battery.
concepts.overview: This claim is the conclusion of the Bosch-versus-Bafang discussion. Battery brand is a weak reason to choose a system, because most makers use cells from the same few suppliers (see [same cells inside every brand](#c/01M3VW6A51H78EJ2A8EF9XSBEB)). What does differ is the support behind the bike: [Bosch and Shimano systems](#c/01M3VW6A51630KP5K96DHA0A42) have a larger dealer network for warranty repairs. For a daily commuter, downtime matters more than any spec, since a bike stuck waiting for a repair means no way to get to work. That reasoning favours the Bosch-based Alder and backs the [decision to go with the Alder C5](#c/01M3VW6A517KMY638Y7HNQY3VA).

concepts.title: Belt drive
concepts.summary: Carbon-reinforced rubber belt replacing the chain: no oil, no rust, lasts 2–3× a chain (about 15,000–20,000 km); needs an internal gear hub.
concepts.overview: A belt drive swaps the metal chain for a carbon-reinforced rubber belt. It needs no oil, does not rust, and lasts two to three times as long as a chain, roughly 15,000 to 20,000 km. The catch is that a belt cannot shift across cassette cogs, so it only works with an [internal gear hub](#c/01M3VW6A4ZK3TSVVEHX6D3AHQ9), which brings fewer gears, slightly more friction, shop-only repairs and a fiddlier flat rear tyre. Here it matters because the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR) is the one bike that has it, and it cuts the [three-year running cost](#c/01M3VW6A50HE7E988Q791BPPFQ) to about 650 against 850 for chain bikes. That is a saving of only about 200, which is why it is a modest advantage rather than a deciding one.

concepts.title: Bafang systems
concepts.summary: Cheaper and more open: cheaper parts, more shops can work on them; less polished power delivery and more variation between bike makers' setups.
concepts.overview: Bafang makes the motor systems used on budget and mid-priced e-bikes, such as the Bafang M400 on the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD). sections.heading: What did the reader need?
sections.md:
The reader commutes 14 km each way, about 6,000 km a year, with one real hill of about 800 m at up to 8 percent. They weigh about 80 kg, carry a laptop bag, and set a budget of up to 3,500. They also did not want to arrive sweaty.

sections.heading: How was the choice narrowed down?
sections.md:
The assistant started with three choices that shape everything else: motor type, battery size and frame style. For the hill and the wish to stay unsweaty, a [mid-drive](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) was judged [the safer bet](#c/01M3VW4MRPEF6FXC20G7PPVN3P). Battery sizing of 400 to 500 Wh suits 28 km a day with a hill.

Four bikes were then offered: the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) (about 3,200, 24 kg), the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR) (about 3,400, 26 kg, belt drive), the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD) (about 2,300, 23 kg) and the [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3VW59EVFKQ96MWZWNKBPFN0) (about 1,700, hub motor). sections.heading: How did the bikes score on the reader's priorities?
sections.md:
The reader ranked their priorities: [hill climbing](#c/01M3VW59EVTDPBDCFA6HP66A99), [low maintenance](#c/01M3VW59EVWQ45SDAZ1Z49QGK9), [weight for the stairs](#c/01M3VW59EVZ9Y69NWVHADKJ165) and [theft resistance](#c/01M3VW59EV784C6QXRWRRR0XS6), with [price](#c/01M3VW59EVWNHX5KEP8B60YQYP) second.

- **Low maintenance**: Birch clearly, with its belt and internal hub.
- **Weight**: Cedar best, Alder close, Birch worst.

- **Price**: Cedar is cheapest by about 1,000.

concepts.title: Mid-drive is the safer bet
concepts.summary: A good hub motor can manage 8% for 800 m at moderate speed, but a mid-drive lets you shift down and keep cadence: less effort, less sweat.
concepts.overview: This is the assistant's verdict on the motor choice once the reader described the hill: about 800 m long, 8 percent at its steepest. A good hub motor could manage that at moderate speed, but a [mid-drive](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) lets the rider shift down and keep cadence, so the effort is lower and there is less sweat. That ties directly to the reader's wish to [arrive without sweating](#c/01M3VW4MRMXKGXJ0AMBXTETEB9). The argument rests on [torque](#c/01M3VW4MRPPQT6XRYW092NBN8G), at 60 to 85 Nm for mid-drives against 40 to 50 Nm for typical [hub motors](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT). It is the reason only mid-drives stayed in contention, and the cheap hub bike was set aside early. Note the claim is about safety margin, not impossibility: a hub motor would cope, with more effort.

sections.heading: What exactly is being claimed?
sections.md:
The claim came in reply to the reader's description of the hill: about 800 m long, maybe 8 percent at the steepest, and a strong wish not to arrive sweaty. The assistant said an 8 percent grade for 800 m is fine for a good hub motor at moderate speed. A mid-drive is still the safer bet because it lets you shift down and keep cadence, which means less effort and less sweat.

So the claim is about margin and rider effort, not about whether a hub motor can physically make the climb.

prov.quote: a mid-drive lets you shift down and keep cadence, which means less effort and less sweat.

sections.heading: Why do the gears matter?
sections.md:
A [mid-drive](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) sits at the pedals and drives the chain, so it works [through the bike's gears](#c/01M3VWEBBMVF5ARPXPSH6ZWNA8). On a climb the rider can drop to an easier gear and keep a steady pedalling rhythm while the motor adds its help. A [hub motor](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT) sits in the wheel and does not use the gears, so it cannot multiply its effort the same way on a long steep slope.

This is why the claim serves the goal to [arrive without sweating](#c/01M3VW4MRMXKGXJ0AMBXTETEB9): the same hill takes less rider effort when the gears are working with the motor.

sections.heading: What does torque say?
sections.md:
The assistant pointed to [torque](#c/01M3VW4MRPPQT6XRYW092NBN8G) as the number to look at. Mid-drives run 60 to 85 Nm: Bosch Performance Line CX 85 Nm, Shimano EP8 85 Nm and Bosch Performance Line 75 Nm. Typical hub motors give 40 to 50 Nm.

The gap is large for an 80 kg rider carrying a laptop bag. The Alder's 75 Nm was later judged plenty for an 8 percent hill.

prov.quote: 60 to 85 Nm for mid-drives

sections.heading: What did it change in the decision?
sections.md:
The claim explains why three of the four bikes compared have mid-drives, and why the hub-motor [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3VW59EVFKQ96MWZWNKBPFN0) was included only "for contrast". It narrowed the field before the reader ranked their priorities, and it feeds into [Go with the Alder C5](#c/01M3VW6A517KMY638Y7HNQY3VA).

The trade-offs of a hub motor were also stated: it is cheaper, quieter and needs less maintenance. The reader accepted the mid-drive anyway, and the [test ride](#c/01M3VW6A52YXHZH1AJX1277NYM) will check how the hill feels in practice.

concepts.title: Mid-drive motor
concepts.summary: Motor at the pedals driving the chain, so it uses the bike's gears; climbs far better and feels natural. Typically 60–85 Nm.
concepts.overview: A mid-drive motor sits at the pedals and drives the chain, which means it works through the bike's own gears. That is why it climbs hills far better than a hub motor and feels natural to ride: you can shift down and keep a steady cadence while the motor adds its torque. Typical mid-drives deliver 60 to 85 Nm, such as the Bosch Performance Line CX and Shimano EP8 at 85 Nm, against 40 to 50 Nm for common hub motors. For this reader, with an 800 m climb at up to 8 percent and a wish to arrive unsweaty, it is the [safer bet](#c/01M3VW4MRPEF6FXC20G7PPVN3P), and it is the alternative to the [hub motor](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT). Three of the four bikes compared use one, including the chosen [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH). The trade-off is a higher price and more maintenance than a hub motor.

sections.heading: How does a mid-drive work?
sections.md: A mid-drive motor is mounted at the bottom bracket, where the pedals attach, and pushes on the chain. The motor therefore uses the bike's gears. The rider can shift down for a hill and keep a comfortable cadence while the motor works at a good speed. That is also why it feels natural: assistance follows the pedalling rather than pushing from the wheel. See [how it drives through the gears](#c/01M3VWEBBMVF5ARPXPSH6ZWNA8).

sections.heading: How does it compare with a hub motor?
sections.md:
The [hub motor](#c/01M3VW4MRN5QN1VWQ4Z2BCYSVT) is the alternative. It sits in the rear or front wheel and is cheaper, quieter and needs less maintenance, but it struggles on long steep climbs.

The main difference is [torque](#c/01M3VW4MRPPQT6XRYW092NBN8G): 60 to 85 Nm for mid-drives (Bosch Performance Line CX 85 Nm, Shimano EP8 85 Nm, Bosch Performance Line 75 Nm) against 40 to 50 Nm for typical hub motors.

sections.heading: Why does it suit this commute?
sections.md:
The route has one 800 m hill at up to 8 percent, and the reader does not want to arrive sweaty. A good hub motor could cope at moderate speed, but the mid-drive lets the rider shift down and keep cadence. That is the reasoning behind [Mid-drive is the safer bet](#c/01M3VW4MRPEF6FXC20G7PPVN3P).

Three of the four bikes compared use a mid-drive: the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) (Bosch Performance Line, 75 Nm), the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR) (Shimano EP6, 85 Nm) and the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD) (Bafang M400, 80 Nm). In the ranking, the Birch and Cedar climb best, and the Alder's 75 Nm is plenty for 8 percent.

sections.heading: What are the costs of choosing one?
sections.md:
Every drive that uses a chain needs chain upkeep. For the chain bikes (Alder and Cedar), the assistant estimated about 850 over three years for chains, cassettes, brake pads and services, at 6,000 km a year. Mid-drive bikes also tend to cost more than the hub-motor option, so price and maintenance are the trade-off for the climbing ability.

The Birch avoids most chain upkeep with a belt and internal hub, at an estimated 650 over three years.

sections.heading: Where do the numbers come from?
sections.md:
The figures are the assistant's rough estimate for the reader's **6,000 km a year**, which follows from 14 km each way on a daily commute. Wear parts are priced per item and then summed over three years.

For the chain bikes ([Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) and [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD)):

- Chains every 3,000 to 4,000 km: about 5 chains at 30
- A cassette every other chain: 2 to 3 at 50
- Brake pads: 4 sets at 25
- Two services a year at 80 each

The total is about **850** over three years.

prov.quote: chains every 3,000 to 4,000 km (about 5 chains, 30 each), a cassette every other chain (2 to 3 at 50)

sections.heading: How does the belt bike compare?
sections.md:
The belt-driven Birch Metro 8 comes to about **650**. A belt is expected to last roughly 15,000 to 20,000 km, so perhaps one belt (90) is needed. Add brake pads, one internal hub service (60) and yearly services.

The gap is about 200, which is why [the belt saves only about 200](#c/01M3VW6A50SW9N8XW6VA4F522F). The [belt drive](#c/01M3VW6A4ZMJQZTS6MHQ460VJS) lowers the total because belt wear is much slower than chain and cassette wear.

A caution: the chat does not itemise the yearly services for the belt bike. The listed items do not clearly add up to 650, so treat it as a rounded estimate.

prov.quote: So the belt saves maybe 200 over three years, not a huge amount.

sections.heading: What is left out?
sections.md:
The three-year totals cover servicing and wear parts only. The [battery](#c/01M3VW6HBZF58ZJP6N0EBHCKTG) is counted separately.

A 500 Wh battery keeps about 80 percent of its capacity after 500 to 800 full cycles. At a full cycle every two days, that is 3 to 4 years. So a replacement costing **600 to 800** may fall near the end of the period. That would raise the real three-year cost for any of the bikes by a similar amount, and it does not change the gap between chain and belt.

sections.heading: What can bring the cost down?
sections.md: Shop terms matter too. The first service is usually free after 500 km, and the battery warranty is usually 2 years, according to the test-ride advice. Both can trim the early costs, so they are worth confirming (see [first service and battery warranty](#c/01M3VW6A527HS27XFC0YN82SMZ)). These terms are typical, not guaranteed, so confirm them with the shop before buying.

concepts.overview: This is where the whole comparison lands: the reader chose the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH) as the best all-rounder for their list. Its Bosch 75 Nm motor is plenty for an 800 m, 8 percent hill, it weighs 24 kg, close to the Cedar and easier on the second-floor stairs than the Birch, and it is the one bike that supports an app motor lock against theft at a work rack. The cost is a chain, so the maintenance is a little higher than on the belt-driven [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR). Since [the belt saves only about 200](#c/01M3VW6A50SW9N8XW6VA4F522F) over three years, that trade is easy to accept. The [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD) stays the fallback if saving about 1,000 matters more. The choice is not final until the [test-ride checklist](#c/01M3VW6A52YXHZH1AJX1277NYM) is done.

sections.md:
After comparing the options, the reader said: "I'll go with the Alder." The choice is the [Alder C5](#c/01M3VW59ETWZN25FX8WQSB16DH), a Bosch 75 Nm mid-drive with a 500 Wh battery, 24 kg, at around 3,200. It answers the question [Which e-bike should I buy?](#c/01M3VW4MRNRXV5FKBXX0X4Q544).

The decision is a working choice, not a final purchase. The test ride may still change it.

sections.heading: Why the Alder fits the reader's priorities
sections.md:
The reader named four priorities, with price second: hill climbing, low maintenance, weight for the stairs, and theft protection. The assistant scored the bikes against them:

- **Hill climbing**: Birch (85 Nm) and Cedar (80 Nm) are strongest. The Alder (75 Nm) is "plenty for 8 percent", so it clears [hill climbing](#c/01M3VW59EVTDPBDCFA6HP66A99).
- **Weight**: Cedar is best, Alder close, Birch worst. That makes the Alder [light enough for the stairs](#c/01M3VW59EVZ9Y69NWVHADKJ165), especially with the 2.5 to 3 kg battery removed.
- **Theft protection**: the Alder is best, because it supports the [app motor lock](#c/01M3VW6A514F2A1300M3DT9SJT), so it improves [theft resistance](#c/01M3VW59EV784C6QXRWRRR0XS6).
- **Low maintenance**: the Birch wins clearly, and the Alder only partly meets [low maintenance](#c/01M3VW59EVWQ45SDAZ1Z49QGK9).

The assistant called it "the best all-rounder for your list".

sections.heading: What was given up, and what were the alternatives?
sections.md:
The cost of choosing the Alder is chain maintenance. Over three years that is about 850 against about 650 for the belt-driven [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3VW59ET5ZZ9SA2MZ0TJHVVR). Because [the belt saves only about 200](#c/01M3VW6A50SW9N8XW6VA4F522F), the gap is small enough to accept. The Birch is also the heaviest of the mid-drives at 26 kg, which counts against it for the stairs.

The assistant laid out the alternatives:

- The **Birch** if maintenance matters more than the stairs.
- The [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3VW59EV4D9RXFW5JH9Y7BGD) if saving about 1,000 matters more.

The Dogwood hub bike was set aside early, in favour of [a mid-drive](#c/01M3VW4MRPEF6FXC20G7PPVN3P) for the hill.

prov.quote: the Birch if maintenance matters more than the stairs; the Cedar if you'd rather save 1,000

sections.heading: Why the dealer network supports the choice
sections.md: The Alder uses a Bosch system. Independent tests generally rate Bosch and Shimano systems as more refined, with a larger dealer network for warranty repairs. The assistant said that for a daily commuter, where downtime matters, "the dealer network is the real point" (see [Dealer network matters most](#c/01M3VW6A5155D0KHWTABVDSBPC)). This backs the Alder, though it is not a claim that Bosch batteries are better.

prov.quote: For a daily commuter where downtime matters, the dealer network is the real point, more than the battery.

sections.heading: What happens next?
sections.md:
The decision leads straight to the [test-ride checklist](#c/01M3VW6A52YXHZH1AJX1277NYM):

1. Ride the hill in the middle assist mode and see whether you would arrive sweaty.
2. Check the frame size.
3. Carry it up a flight of stairs with the battery out.
4. Ask about [the first service and battery warranty](#c/01M3VW6A527HS27XFC0YN82SMZ).
5. Try the motor lock in the app before buying.

Lock choice and insurance are recommended but not decided: a Sold Secure Gold or Diamond D-lock plus a cable, and insurance of about 100 to 150 a year.

concepts.overview: The Alder C5 is the bike the reader chose, and it was one of three serious contenders. It pairs a Bosch Performance Line mid-drive (75 Nm) with a 500 Wh battery, a 10-speed chain, mudguards and a rack, weighs 24 kg, and costs around 3,200. Its 75 Nm is the lowest of the three mid-drives but still plenty for this commute's 8 percent hill. It is light enough to carry up to a second-floor flat, and its distinctive strength is the [app motor lock](#c/01M3VW6A514F2A1300M3DT9SJT), which can disable the motor when the bike is left at a work rack. Because it is a chain bike, it only partly meets the low-maintenance wish compared with the belt-driven Birch. It is an example of a [mid-drive motor](#c/01M3VW4MRNJEBZQR4RT4S4ZH9Z) and is the bike behind the [decision to go with it](#c/01M3VW6A517KMY638Y7HNQY3VA).
